2 Billionaire Funds Dumped AMD Last Quarter. Is It a Sell?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) has been a fantastic stock to own in 2026. The stock has risen around 100% so far, though it was up 200% at the start of October. AMD became a popular choice for many investors, including the smart money in hedge funds. However, now that the latest round of 13-F filings has come out, it's clear that selling AMD has become a trend among fund managers.

Two major funds sold all of their shares during the third quarter: Appaloosa Management, run by David Tepper, and Coatue Management, run by Philippe Laffont. When giant funds like this sell, it's normally time to start thinking about selling your shares as well. So, is it time to move on from AMD stock?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

AMD is doing well as a business

First, let's tackle the business. AMD has always played second fiddle to Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) in the data center industry, as Nvidia's hardware and software have always been a step ahead of AMD's. However, AMD's products are becoming more popular among certain customers because they are cheaper. While they may not be as capable, power-efficient, or user-friendly, they can be quite useful if they're not being tasked with a wide variety of operations.

This has led to more adoption of AMD's products, and AMD's Q3 results back that up. The company experienced 97% year-over-year revenue growth in its data center division to $8.5 billion during Q3. However, AMD is more than just a data center company. Its overall growth rate was 45% year-over-year to $11.5 billion, as its client and gaming segment decreased year-over-year, partially offset by increasing Embedded processors doing well. Overall, those are solid results for AMD, but there's just one problem: It's far smaller than Nvidia.

AMD already has a tough enough time being compared to Nvidia's products. For it to be a better investment than Nvidia, it should be showing stronger growth, but it's not. During its fiscal third quarter (ended in October), Nvidia's overall revenue rose 103% year over year to nearly $116 billion. So, Nvidia is 10 times larger than AMD. On the data center side, Nvidia's revenue rose 110% to $108 billion.

Nvidia has the technology edge and the growth edge. However, AMD has dramatically outperformed Nvidia this year, and there is one obvious reason for that: valuation.

Altimeter's Brad Gerstner Says Nvidia Was Priced for "Negative Growth for 2028 and 2029." Wall Street Expects 29% ©@jiefeng jiang from Getty Images via Canva, @metamorworks from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) jumped 31.5% on Monday after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, but it still traded at about 11x forward earnings at the close.

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner says that multiple priced in shrinking growth for 2028 and 2029, while analysts expect revenue and earnings to keep climbing.

The main risk is that hyperscalers have stopped raising their capex forecasts, which matters for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM:NYSE) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) too.

The stock depends on its 2028 estimates holding, and the hyperscalers' reports in late January and early February are the next test.

NVIDIA jumped 31.5% on Monday, Nov. 23, after its board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after he resigned.

But Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner thinks the bigger story is how cheap the stock got before the jump.

On Monday's Halftime Report, Gerstner said that as of that morning, "what was imputed into the NVIDIA multiple was actually negative growth for 2028 and 2029. I think it's nuts."

Wall Street expects the opposite.

And NVIDIA isn't the only one with a lot riding on 2028. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) and AMD need those years to hold too.

Wall Street still sees growth in both years

On CNBC's Power Lunch, Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said the Street expects NVIDIA's revenue to grow 72% in calendar 2027 and 29% in calendar 2028.

TIKR's consensus has revenue more than doubling, from $424 billion in the year ending January 2027 to $927 billion in the year ending January 2029:

Nvidia (NVDA): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to January) (TIKR)

Earnings follow the same path. Analysts expect normalized EPS to climb 31%, from $16.61 in the year ending January 2028 to $21.77 the year after:

Nvidia (NVDA): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to January) (TIKR)
The market is priced for a peak

Now look at what investors pay for that growth. Even after Monday's jump, NVIDIA traded at about 11x forward earnings at the close. That's up from a five-year low of 8.7x on Friday, but far below its five-year average of 35x and its peak of nearly 70x in May 2023:

NVIDIA (NVDA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

A multiple that low only makes sense if investors expect those 2028 estimates to be cut hard, as if this cycle peaks in 2027.

Capex forecasts have stopped rising

The worry is NVIDIA's customers. As Wedbush's Matt Bryson put it on CNBC's Closing Bell, "it feels like the entire AI trade is assuming that there's deterioration either in 27 or 28."

Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Marvell Technology reports its fiscal third quarter on Tuesday, Dec 1, after the market close. That quarter is part of fiscal 2027, the year ending January 2027. Analysts expect revenue of about $3.15 billion. But Marvell has already said revenue came in line with its guide, so the fourth-quarter outlook is likely to move the stock most.

That estimate matches Marvell's own forecast. On its Aug 27 call, Marvell guided to $3.15 billion at the midpoint, plus or minus 5%. On Nov 2, it said preliminary revenue was in line with that guide and narrowed the range to plus or minus 2%, or about $3.09 billion to $3.21 billion. So the quarter's revenue is largely known. Marvell said it expects growth to speed up again in the fourth quarter.

Other chip stocks often move the same way, but by much less. Nvidia moved in Marvell's direction on 10 of the days after its last 12 reports. AMD did so 9 times and Broadcom 8 times. Their average moves were only 2% to 3%, ignoring direction.

How far has Marvell fallen before this report?

Marvell closed at $131.57 on Tuesday, Nov 24. It fell 9.1% that day. The S&P 500 slipped 0.50%, and the Nasdaq-100 dropped 2.0%. Other chip stocks fell as well. Advanced Micro Devices lost 8.9%, Nvidia 5.9% and Broadcom 4.0%.

The longer slide is steeper. Marvell is 58.4% below its record close of $316.43 on Thursday, June 4. Since its last report day, Aug 27, it has lost 45.5%. It also fell 12.7% on Nov 2, the day it announced an all-stock deal to acquire Lumentum.

Marvell has lost 45.5% since its last report day. If you sold some shares before that fall, or are holding cash until the report, that money can still earn something while it waits. The stock is still up 54.8% in 2026. Buyers left as chip stocks sold off together, and the Lumentum deal brought a sharp fall of its own. What would bring them back, in our view, is revenue near the top of the narrowed range and a fourth-quarter outlook that backs up the promised speed-up.

What is Marvell promising for the rest of the year?

The $3.15 billion midpoint, which analysts also expect, would be 51.8% above the same quarter a year earlier. Marvell also said it expected its data center revenue to grow more than 20% from the prior quarter and roughly 75% from a year earlier.

Trading volume reached 356.8 million shares, coming in about 91% above its three-month average of 186.5 million shares. Nvidia IPO'd in 1999 and has grown 363,896% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 closed at 7,183, down 0.25%, while the Nasdaq Composite finished at 23,586, down 0.62%. Among semiconductors and AI computing platforms, Advanced Micro Devices closed at $406.03, down 1.75%, and Broadcom closed at $300.86, down 0.07%, highlighting broad pressure across chip names.

What this means for investors

The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose by a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual rate in October. That was in line with estimates, but nearly twice the Federal Reserve's target. That had investors selling tech stocks with another interest rate hike seemingly more likely.

Nvidia stock itself has many underlying currents, though. Investors are trimming AI exposure as spending worries and inflation fears weigh on Nvidia and other chip names. New tariff proposals added to the angst.

At the same time, investors are balancing the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with ongoing risks related to the investigations into his actions and the company's export controls. The reaction suggests investors remain cautious, despite the strong earnings and guidance.

Investors need to balance risks against business potential and should make appropriate allocations based on both.

By the closing bell, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average had rallied for a 0.3% gain to 50,182. But the broad-based S&P 500 was still down 0.3% at 7,182, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite had given back 0.6% to 23,585.

What Happened In Chip Stocks On Monday?

Monday's rise came one session after a rough Friday for Qualcomm.

Hyperscalers are the largest cloud computing companies.

Was It Qualcomm Or Its Group?

It was the group. Among the other semiconductor companies worth $2 billion or more, the median gain was 14.1%. In all, 29 of the 33 rose by 5% or more. Qualcomm rose with its group, but its 10.3% gain was well below that 14.1% median.

Every company on Trefis's peer list for Qualcomm rose too. They are NVIDIA, Intel, Texas Instruments, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom. Intel gained 16.3%, while Broadcom rose 3%.

Where Does Qualcomm Stock Stand After The Rise?

A rise like this is not rare for Qualcomm. It had 4 sessions with a rise at least this large in the past year. The latest session with a move this large in either direction was a fall of 11.1% on October 30.

Monday's close of $165.38 sits well below its highest close of the past 12 months, $251.02 on May 29. The past six months were hard. title: David Tepper Sold All of His AMD Stock. His Biggest Position Is Micron.
detail:
David Tepper Sold All of His AMD Stock. His Biggest Position Is Micron.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 1:20 PM CST 5 min read
NVDA
MU
AMD
ANT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

There has been a ton of news in the stock market recently. Nvidia is making headlines with its CEO controversy and third-quarter earnings. Newly public Anthropic went public with a lot of fanfare. However, there was another event that occurred this week that flew under the radar of most investors: 13-F releases.

While looking at Security and Exchange Commission (SEC) documents may sound a tad boring, these documents reveal what trades billionaire hedge fund managers made in the third quarter. Those are valuable pieces of information, as they show what the smart money is doing.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

One billionaire that I follow is David Tepper and his fund, Appaloosa Management. Tepper made some interesting moves during Q3. The most noteworthy was loading up on Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) shares while completely exiting his Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) position.

That's quite the call, but is it the right one?

David Tepper. Image source: Getty Images.

Selling AMD during Q3 was a wise move

Information available from 13-Fs naturally lags the market. The SEC requires funds with over $100 million in investments to disclose their end-of-quarter holdings and make those public 45 days after the quarter ends. This gives some buffer between filing and release date, which protects the fund's investments.

However, investors need to be careful not to follow these documents too closely, as the landscape may have shifted from the end of the quarter to now.

AMD is in that boat, because it has lost about 20% of its value since Q3 ended. That justifies Tepper's move and makes it appear that his fund took gains before a sell-off occurred. The reason? Likely AMD's valuation.

AMD's stock has had a great year this year, but not all of that success has come from business growth. Instead, the market has chosen to give AMD a far higher premium this year than it has in the past. Reaching about 35 times next year's earnings at the end of Q3, it signaled that it was time to sell the stock.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

Tepper did exactly that, and I think that was a smart move, because there was just too much hype baked into AMD's stock price. Buying Micron was an interesting pivot, and I think it may turn out to be the right move.

Micron's stock is incredibly cheap

AMD stock could reward patient investors enormously

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is entering another defining stretch in 2026, as record financial results and growing artificial intelligence demand put its growth ambitions under closer scrutiny.

The AI chipmaker continues to secure major hyperscaler contracts and deliver stronger numbers, reinforcing expectations that its expansion has further room to run.

That momentum has also pushed shares toward levels that leave investors weighing how much future growth is already reflected in the stock.

Despite those concerns, Wall Street sees further upside, raising a bigger question about whether AMD can deliver enough growth to justify its rising valuation.

Also Read: AMD stock jumps 13% after 5-star analyst resets price target

AMD's record quarter cements its data center pivot

AMD's third-quarter revenue reached $13.4 billion, up 45% annually on record Instinct graphics processing unit (GPU) and EPYC processor sales.

Non-generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $2.09, beating Wall Street's $1.95 estimate, according to CNBC, while GAAP net income reached $2.4 billion for the quarter.

Jean Hu, chief financial officer at AMD, attributed the 74% increase in non-GAAP EPS to operating leverage, as data center scale continues to expand across cloud customers.

Revenue exceeded the high end of AMD's guidance for the quarter, giving management credibility heading into the 2027 planning cycle.

Data center revenue hit $8.5 billion, up 97% from a year ago, and now accounts for roughly 64% of total sales, up from 47% last year.

Operating income reached $2.8 billion on a GAAP basis, supported by scale leverage and a growing mix of higher-margin data center products.

Free cash flow for the quarter came in at $554 million, down from $1.53 billion a year earlier, as inventory and receivables built ahead of a guided $17 billion fourth quarter.

AMD's long-term AI playbook stretches beyond 2027

AMD's management outlined one of the most aggressive growth frameworks in the semiconductor industry at its November 2025 Financial Analyst Day.

The company is targeting compound annual revenue growth above 35% over the next three to five years, with the data center segment compounding above 60%.
